title: Year one, you are the function
summary: Twelve quarters from a single architect in a greenfield to an enterprise architecture function with its own team, budget, and mandate. What to ship each quarter, which forum to open when, when to federate instead of hire, how the money moves from someone else's budget to your own, and the signals that say slow down.
html:
The job offer says enterprise architect, singular. You arrive to find a greenfield or something close to it: a company that has grown fast, an IT organization that has been shipping without a map, and a CTO who hired you because something told them the next three years cannot be run the way the last three were. There is no board, no repository, no standards, no team, and no budget line with your name on it.

Everything is a priority, which means nothing is. The temptation, felt in the first fortnight, is to design the target operating model - to draw the function you eventually want, org chart and all, and present it in month two. I have done this. It gets polite nods and changes nothing, because an organization does not fund a structure it has never felt the absence of.

Nobody funds an architecture function. They fund the second year of one that has already been useful.

What follows is a twelve-quarter build, composited from my own missions and from watching other people's first years go well and badly. Company sizes blur, figures are rounded, and any resemblance to a specific initiative is the resemblance all of these have to each other. Adjust the pace to your context: a five-hundred-person company moves faster through year one than a five-thousand-person one, and a regulated industry moves slower through year two than anyone would like.

The shape of the climb#

Three years, three different jobs. Year one you are the function - a single practitioner whose output is artifacts and rescued projects, not governance. Year two you federate - the practice starts running through people who do not report to you, and you make your first two hires. Year three you become a function - own team, own cost center, own service catalog, and, if it went well, a successor who could run it without you.

Four principles hold across all twelve quarters, and I would defend each of them in an argument.

Ship an artifact every quarter that outlives you. Not a deck - an artifact someone else uses when you are on holiday: an inventory, a pattern, a decision log, a template. Twelve quarters, twelve artifacts, and by year three the practice has a body that is not your body.

Borrow before you hire. Every hour you can get from a solution architect, a lead engineer, or a domain expert is an hour that costs no headcount and creates an ally. The federation in year two is not a compromise you make because you cannot hire; it is the better design, and the hires exist to serve it.

Governance follows usefulness, never the other way round. Every rule you introduce should be answering a pain the organization has already felt. Introduce the design forum after the third integration mess, not before the first.

Never ask for budget you cannot spend well. A function that returns unspent headcount in year two does not get it back in year three.

Year one: the practitioner#

The whole year is about earning the right to have a second year. You will spend it doing architecture work that looks suspiciously like consulting, and that is correct.

Q1 - Look, do not organize. Meet everyone who builds or buys anything, and walk the landscape properly rather than sending a survey - the due diligence method is exactly this phase, compressed. Draw the first coarse capability map, two levels, and get one business leader to say out loud that it describes their world. Pick up one live technical problem and solve it, personally, visibly, this quarter. That solved problem is your entry ticket; the map is your instrument.

The artifact that ships: a capability map and a first-pass inventory, however ugly. The forum you open: none. You have no standing yet, and a governance meeting in Q1 will be remembered as the moment architecture became overhead. The money: zero of your own. The only rule you introduce is the one you apply to yourself - write down every decision you make, numbered, in a place people can find.

Q2 - Make the inventory true, and pick the line. Turn the collection into a real inventory with owners, and settle the application versus IT component question in writing before anyone has strong feelings about it. This is the cheapest quarter of your entire career to make that decision, and the one with the longest compounding.

Artifact: the classification policy on one page, plus the inventory with a minimum data standard. Forum: still none, but start a fortnightly thirty-minute conversation with each of the two or three heaviest-building teams - not a review, a conversation, in their calendar not yours. Governance: the definition-of-done rule quietly appears in one project's closing checklist, with the project manager's blessing rather than a mandate. Money: still none, though you will spend a small tooling budget from the CTO's pocket if you need a repository. Resist buying an expensive one this year - a spreadsheet you keep honest beats a platform you cannot fill, and the starter kit for running it that way is free.

Q3 - Solve something expensive, then name the pattern. Somewhere in the landscape is a recurring, costly mistake - the same integration built four ways, the same authentication problem re-solved per team. Fix one instance with the team, then write the pattern down and put your name on the shape rather than the fix. Patterns are how a single person scales before they have anyone to scale through.

Artifact: the first two or three reference patterns, each a page, each with a worked example from your own landscape. Forum: open the design conversation - a weekly, engineer-level hour where anyone can bring a design. Keep it advisory, no gates, no approvals; you are building the habit, not the checkpoint. Governance: none new. Money: make a note of every hour you spend firefighting; you will need that number in Q4.

Q4 - Show the year, ask for the next one. Write the year-one review the CTO can forward upward without editing: what existed at the start, what exists now, three things that did not go wrong because of the work, and the two or three that did because the work did not exist yet. Then make the year-two ask, and make it small enough to be granted: one hire, a named budget line, and a mandate for a design forum with teeth.

Artifact: the year-one review and a one-page architecture operating model - not an org chart, a description of how decisions will get made next year. Forum: the design forum becomes formal, with a standing slot and a light pre-read expectation. Governance: agree the first two-gate skeleton for large projects only. Money: this is the quarter you ask for a line inside the CTO's budget rather than a function of your own.

Year one has one deliverable that matters: a CTO who can explain, unprompted, what architecture does here.

Year two: federate, then hire#

Year two is where most functions go wrong in one of two directions. Either they hire fast and build a central team that becomes the department everyone routes around, or they stay solo out of modesty and burn out the one person who knows how everything fits.

The way through is federation first, hiring second. Federation means the practice runs through people who do not report to you: a named architect inside each significant domain, doing eighty percent delivery and twenty percent architecture, connected by a guild you run.

The bargain is explicit, and I put it in writing every time. The domain architect gets: the title, a seat at the board, first access to patterns and to my time, and a development path that leads somewhere. Their line manager gets: a person who solves architecture problems in their own domain instead of waiting for central. I get: reach I could never hire, and the truth about what is happening in each domain, faster than any report. What I do not get is control over their objectives - and pretending otherwise is how these arrangements die.

Two rules keep federation from becoming a fiction. Their architecture time is named in their objectives, agreed with their line manager, and it is a fifth of their capacity, not a rounding error. And there is one quality gate that is mine: the pattern conformance of what they design, checked in the design forum, not in a private conversation.

Q5 - Name the domain architects. Three or four, no more, chosen for credibility with their peers rather than for architectural purity - you can teach patterns, you cannot teach standing. Run the first guild session: ninety minutes a fortnight, half of it working on real designs together, half on the practice itself. Artifact: the domain architect role description and the twenty-percent agreement, signed by line managers. Governance: the design forum gains its first gate - direction checks for anything above a size threshold.

Q6 - Open the board. With three or four federated architects and a design forum that people actually attend, you finally have the raw material for an architecture board that will not be routed around. Launch it on two real, burning decisions. Artifact: the board charter and the decision record format, live from session one. Governance: the second gate arrives, and the exception register opens - with expiries from the very first entry, because an exception register retrofitted with expiries is a year of arguments.

Q7 - The first hire, and it is probably not who you think. The instinct is to hire another enterprise architect in your own image. In most cases the higher-leverage first hire is the person who makes the practice run: someone who owns the repository, the inventory quality loop, the board secretariat, and the reporting. Call it an architecture office role, an APM lead, whatever fits your grades. That hire buys back the day a week you are losing to administration, and it makes every other person's output visible. My second hire is usually a solution architect for the busiest domain, because that is where delivery pressure is breaking the federation model.

Artifact: the portfolio quality operating loop - triggers, cadence, KPIs - handed to the new hire as their first ownership. Money: this is the quarter your budget stops being invisible. You now have named lines inside the CTO's budget: two heads, the repository tooling, a training and certification line for the federated architects, and a small advisory line for the two or three questions a year where an outside opinion is genuinely cheaper than an internal argument.

Q8 - Rate the portfolio, and let the numbers do the arguing. With an honest inventory and a working board, run the first business fit and technical fit assessment across the domains. The output is not a rating exercise; it is your first budget-grade artifact - a portfolio view that says where the money should go next year, in the language the CFO's people already speak.

Artifact: the portfolio assessment and the first target-state diagrams per domain, dated and attached to board records. Forum: the quarterly session begins - the one where receiving teams score their own architecture key results in public. Governance: the definition of done now includes repository updates across all projects, enforced by the PMO rather than requested by you.

Year three: a function with its own name#

The transition that matters in year three is not organizational, it is financial. A function that lives inside someone else's budget can be helpful; a function with its own cost center can plan. And you cannot plan a two-year platform migration from a line item that gets renegotiated whenever the CTO's budget is squeezed.

The argument that wins is never "architecture deserves a budget". It is a portfolio of concrete numbers you have been quietly collecting since year one: the duplicate systems the board prevented or retired, the run cost the consolidation decisions removed, the projects that passed a gate with a design change that avoided a rebuild, and the rework you can attribute to architecture not existing in year one. Two or three real cases, honestly quantified with ranges, beat any maturity model slide ever produced.

Q9 - Package the practice as services. Write the architecture service catalog: what teams can ask you for, what each service costs in effort, what they get, and what the turnaround is. This document does more for your legitimacy than any charter, because it converts architecture from a gatekeeper into something you can request. Artifact: the service catalog. Governance: introduce the fast lane in the design forum - pattern-conforming work skips the queue, which is the reward that makes patterns spread on their own.

Q10 - Ask for the cost center, with a plan behind it. Bring the budget case: headcount for the coming year, tooling, training for the federation, a small innovation and evaluation line, and the service catalog as the description of what the money buys. Ask for a three-year envelope rather than an annual one if your organization allows it - platform decisions do not fit in twelve months, and an EA function funded annually will keep making annual-sized decisions.

Artifact: the three-year architecture plan tied to the portfolio assessment. Forum: none new. Governance: the annual charter review - reread the whole thing aloud with the board and delete one rule that has not earned its keep.

Q11 - Hire into the shape, not the wish list. With the cost center approved, hire deliberately: usually a second solution architect for the domain the federation cannot cover, and - if the landscape justifies it - a specialist for the thing that keeps appearing in every decision, which in the last few years has generally meant data or integration. Keep the centre small. The right shape at the end of year three is a centre of three to five people plus five or six federated architects, not a department of twelve.

Artifact: onboarding path for architects - the thing that lets the practice survive a departure. Governance: rotate the moderator role and one domain architect seat; a practice that only works when specific individuals are present is not a function yet.

Q12 - Prove it can run without you. Hand the board chair to someone else for a session. Let a domain architect present the quarterly review. Publish the annual architecture report - decisions made, exceptions closed, portfolio movement, KPIs against targets, and what failed. Then write down what you would tell your successor, and notice how much of it is now written elsewhere anyway.

The money, in plainer terms#

Three funding stages, and each has a different conversation attached.

Invisible (year one). Your salary sits in the CTO's line and you spend nothing. Everything you need, you borrow. The conversation to have in Q4 is not about money at all - it is about whether the CTO can articulate your value without your help.

Named lines (year two). Heads, tooling, training, advisory. Modest numbers, real names. The rule I follow: never ask for a line you cannot show a plan for within the same quarter, and never let the training line be the first thing you sacrifice - it is the only thing you have to offer the federated architects who work for you without reporting to you.

Own cost center (year three). Headcount, tooling, training, evaluation, and ideally a small transformation-support envelope. What changes is not the total, which will still be small next to any delivery budget. What changes is that you can now commit to multi-year moves and be held to them, which is the actual definition of a function.

One practical warning, learned the expensive way: the quarter you receive your own budget is the quarter people start attaching things to you - the "architecture also owns tooling governance, and licensing, and the CMDB" conversation. Some of that is legitimate scope. Some is other people's unloved work looking for a home. The service catalog is your defence: if it is not in the catalog, it is a new service with a new cost, discussed at planning, not absorbed in a corridor.

Where this goes wrong#

Four failure modes, all of which I have either lived through or watched from close enough to feel it.

Hiring before federating. A central team of five architects with no domain relationships produces beautiful target architectures that delivery teams treat as literature. Federation first is not a budget compromise; it is what makes central architecture legible to the people who build.

Governance before credibility. The board opened in Q2 of year one is a board full of people wondering why they are there. The forums in this plan open in a deliberate order - conversation, then design forum, then gates, then board - and each one opens only after the previous has run long enough to have a queue.

The map that ate the year. Capability modelling can absorb infinite time. Two levels, business sign-off, move on. You will improve it in year two with real data, and improving it then is cheap because the argument is about evidence rather than taxonomy.

Confusing the org chart with the function. The reason to want a team is throughput, not status. I have seen a function get its headcount and immediately become slower, because the new people needed onboarding, work needed distributing, and the one person who used to just fix things was now managing. Plan for a productivity dip in the two quarters after each hire. It is real, it is temporary, and pretending it will not happen is how you miss your year-three commitments.

And the signal to slow down, in any quarter: if you cannot name the pain that the next thing you are about to introduce is answering, do not introduce it. Wait a quarter. The pain will arrive, and then the introduction will be welcomed instead of tolerated.

If you only remember the sequence#

Look before you organize. Make the inventory true and draw the classification line early. Solve something expensive, then name the pattern. Show the year and ask small. Federate before you hire, and write the bargain down. Open the board when you have material for it, not when the charter is ready. Hire the person who makes the practice run before you hire your own reflection. Rate the portfolio and let the numbers argue. Package the practice as services. Ask for the cost center with three years of plan behind it. Hire into the shape. Then step back, on purpose, and see whether it holds.

Three years is not long for this. It is also not a schedule anyone will enforce on you: nobody is going to tell you that quarter seven was the moment to hire, or that the board should have opened in quarter six. The only enforcement is the compounding, and the compounding is unforgiving in one direction and generous in the other. A quarter where you shipped something that outlives you makes the next twelve easier. A quarter spent perfecting a model nobody asked for is gone.

The function you want at the end of year three does not look like the one you would have drawn in month two. It is smaller in the middle, larger at the edges, and its authority comes from being useful in a hundred small documented ways rather than from a mandate. That is the version that survives the next reorganization, which is the only durability test that has ever mattered.
